# 1 Maccabees Chapter 11 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17 | **Verses:** 74 | **Disagreements:** 38

---

## Summary
Chapter 11 is complex diplomatic and military narrative. Disagreements cluster around Ptolemy's treachery narrative (vv.1-13), the political vocabulary of the letters (vv.30-37), and the dramatic Antioch battle scene (vv.44-51).

---

## Disagreements

**v.1** — "like the sand by the seashore" (EMET) vs. "as many as the sand on the seashore" (LOGOS) vs. "countless as sand on a beach" (PNEUMA) — classic biblical simile handled differently.

**v.1** — "sought by treachery to gain" (EMET) vs. "scheming by treachery to seize" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "scheming to swallow whole" (PNEUMA)

**v.2** — "with peaceful words" (EMET) vs. "with friendly overtures" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — "overtures" preferred for diplomatic register.

**v.4** — "suburbs destroyed" (EMET) vs. "ruins of Azotus and its suburbs" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) — EMET preserves the parallelism more fully.

**v.5** — "to blame him" (EMET) vs. "to discredit him" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "to get Jonathan in trouble" (PNEUMA)
- "but the king said nothing" (EMET) vs. "the king kept silence" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "The king said nothing" (PNEUMA)

**v.6** — "with glory" (EMET) vs. "with pomp" (LOGOS) vs. "with full ceremony" (PNEUMA) vs. "with full honor" (SOPHIA) — four distinct renderings.

**v.8** — "devising evil plans against Alexander" (EMET/SOPHIA) vs. "plotting evil against Alexander" (LOGOS) vs. "already plotting to take everything" (PNEUMA)

**v.11** — "he was false about him" (EMET) vs. "he slandered Alexander" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "It was a lie" (PNEUMA) — EMET preserves archaic form; LOGOS/SOPHIA use "slandered."

**v.13** — "set on his head the crown of Asia" (EMET) vs. "put on the crown of Asia" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "walked into Antioch and put on the crown of Asia" (PNEUMA)

**v.18** — "those in the fortresses were destroyed by those who were in the fortresses" (EMET) — this difficult phrase: LOGOS "the garrisons in the fortresses were destroyed by those inside"; PNEUMA simplifies to "The fortresses fell to their own garrisons."

**v.19** — PNEUMA converts regnal year to "145 BCE"; others retain regnal year.

**v.20** — "gathered those in Judea" (EMET) vs. "mustered the men of Judea" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "mobilized Judea's forces" (PNEUMA)

**v.22** — "and immediately when he heard it he came" (EMET — preserves the emphatic repetition) vs. "as soon as he heard it, he came" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) — the Greek doubles the participle for urgency.

**v.23** — "put himself in danger" (EMET) vs. "took a risk" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — EMET more literal.

**v.27** — "gave him in gift the revenues of the first rank among the king's friends" (EMET) vs. "had him registered as one of the king's chief friends and awarded him first rank" (LOGOS) vs. "formally registered him among the king's chief friends, first rank" (SOPHIA) — structurally complex verse.

**v.28** — "made him give Israel freedom from tribute" (EMET) vs. "make Judea free from tribute" (LOGOS) vs. "to free Judea from tribute" (SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — "Israel" (EMET) vs. "Judea" (others).

**v.30-37** — The embedded letter: all translators maintain the formal epistolary format, but PNEUMA introduces explanatory expansions ("in lieu of the annual royal revenues previously collected from the land and its orchards" for the produce clause in v.34).

**v.34** — "all their appurtenances" (EMET) vs. "all their dependencies" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — archaic vs. standard.

**v.35** — "tithes and tolls that are due to us" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "tithes and customs duties" (PNEUMA) — "tolls" vs. "customs duties."

**v.38** — "foreign troops which he had recruited from the isles of the nations" (EMET) vs. "foreign mercenaries from the islands of the nations" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "foreign mercenaries from overseas" (PNEUMA)
- "forces of his predecessors hated him" — all agree; PNEUMA adds "veterans of."

**v.39** — "who had been on Alexander's side" (EMET) vs. "who had previously been on Alexander's side" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "one of Alexander's old supporters" (PNEUMA)

**v.40** — "he urged him and said" (EMET) vs. "he pressed him, saying" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "he said" (PNEUMA omits the pressing)

**v.43** — "all my forces have revolted" (EMET) vs. "all my forces have mutinied" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — "mutinied" preferred for military context.

**v.44** — "the king was glad at their coming" (EMET) vs. "the king was overjoyed at their arrival" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "the king's immense relief" (PNEUMA adds emotional color).

**v.45** — "those in the city gathered together — about one hundred and twenty thousand men" — all agree on number; PNEUMA adds "civilians."

**v.46** — "occupied the main streets" (EMET) vs. "seized the main streets" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "took the streets" (PNEUMA)

**v.47** — "dispersed throughout the city" (EMET) vs. "spread through the city" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "spread out through every quarter" (PNEUMA)

**v.48** — "saved the king" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "rescued the king" (SOPHIA/PNEUMA)

**v.50** — "Give us your right hand" (EMET) vs. "Give us terms" (LOGOS) vs. "Give us terms. Give us peace — we surrender." (PNEUMA) — LOGOS/SOPHIA omit the right-hand idiom; EMET preserves it.

**v.51** — "cast down his arms" (EMET) vs. "laid down his arms" (LOGOS) vs. "stood down" (PNEUMA) vs. "laid down his weapons" (SOPHIA)

**v.53** — "lied about all that he had said" (EMET) vs. "broke all his promises" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — EMET more literal to the Greek.

**v.57** — "four districts" — all agree; the fourth district is not explicitly named in the text.

**v.58** — "a dinner service" (EMET/LOGOS) vs. "a full table service" (PNEUMA) vs. "a dinner service" (SOPHIA)
- "golden brooch" — agreement; consistent with ch.10 ruling.

**v.59** — "Ladder of Tyre" — all preserve the toponym.

**v.60** — "cities beyond the River" (EMET) vs. "cities of Trans-Euphrates" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "Trans-Euphrates cities" (PNEUMA) — standard toponym rendered variously.

**v.62** — "gave them his right hand" — all preserve the diplomatic gesture.

**v.67** — "water of Gennesareth" (EMET) vs. "waters of Gennesareth" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "Sea of Galilee" (PNEUMA — uses common name)

**v.68** — "laid an ambush for him in the mountains" (EMET) vs. "set an ambush in the hills" (LOGOS/SOPHIA) vs. "burst out of the hills on their flanks" (PNEUMA combines v.68-69)

**v.70** — "commanders of the forces of the army" (EMET) vs. "commanders of the forces" (LOGOS/SOPHIA/PNEUMA) — minor redundancy in EMET.

**v.71** — "put earth on his head" — all preserve; classic mourning rite.
